strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: rigid pixel/voxel-aligned primitive placement. The proposed sub-pixel heatmap-based primitive detection is technically well motivated and a natural but nontrivial adaptation of keypoint localization ideas to Gaussian allocation.

The method is coherent end to end: VGGT provides pose/depth, the decoder detects off-grid primitive centers, adaptive density allocates more primitives to high-entropy patches, and learned confidence enables multi-view pruning. These components fit the stated goal of improving quality while reducing primitive count.

Empirical results are generally strong. On DL3DV, the method outperforms the compared pose-free feed-forward 3DGS baselines on most metrics while using substantially fewer Gaussians. The ablations support the importance of detection, adaptive density, and confidence-based aggregation, especially for SSIM/LPIPS and artifact reduction.

The paper provides useful analysis beyond image metrics, including geometry/camera-pose evaluation on Charge and qualitative evidence that rendering-based self-supervised fine-tuning can improve VGGT pose estimates rather than merely degrade geometry.

The manuscript is mostly clear, with good diagrams and intuitive visualizations of heatmap specialization, confidence maps, and extrapolated views. The limitations section acknowledges the visible-surface-only failure mode common to feed-forward sparse-view methods.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol for pose-free novel view synthesis is somewhat problematic: target camera poses are obtained via a second forward pass that includes the target images. Even if this follows AnySplat, it means the target image participates in pose estimation, which complicates claims about pure novel-view rendering from only context images and may leak scene/appearance information through the pose-estimation backbone.

The strongest claims about state-of-the-art performance are not uniformly supported. On Charge sparse-view settings, the method often underperforms VGGT+DepthSplat in PSNR and sometimes SSIM, with the explanation attributed to crop/context differences. This is plausible but weakens the blanket claim of superior pose-free feed-forward NVS.

Efficiency claims are only partially substantiated. The paper reports many fewer primitives, but does not provide a sufficiently detailed runtime, memory, rendering speed, or training/inference cost comparison. Since the method relies on VGGT-1B and training uses a 140GB GPU, practical efficiency and accessibility remain unclear.

Reproducibility is incomplete. Important training details such as loss weights, schedules, optimizer settings, dataset subset sizes, sampling proportions, and exact preprocessing are not fully specified in the main text/supplement. Fixed adaptive-density thresholds and entropy choices are also not justified or stress-tested.

The ablation study is helpful but limited. It averages over DL3DV only, does not isolate the teacher-geometry losses and rendering losses in detail, and does not test sensitivity to the number of primitives per density level or confidence pruning threshold.

The method remains heavily dependent on a large supervised 3D foundation model. The paper frames the rendering loop as a promising self-supervised path for geometry improvement, but the evidence is incremental fine-tuning of VGGT rather than training such models without labels, so that broader claim should be tempered.

strengths: The paper addresses a real limitation of feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: rigid pixel- or voxel-aligned primitive layouts can be wasteful and visually artifact-prone. The proposed sub-pixel, patch-wise primitive detection is a plausible and well-motivated alternative.

The method is technically coherent: the decoder uses differentiable soft-argmax/DSNT-style heatmaps, VGGT depth/camera predictions for unprojection, learned confidence for multi-view fusion, and rendering losses with geometry regularization. The overall pipeline is understandable.

The reported results show useful empirical signals: on DL3DV the method generally improves PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS over the compared pose-free feed-forward 3DGS baselines while using substantially fewer primitives; qualitative figures also support cleaner geometry and sharper detail than AnySplat in selected examples.

The ablation study provides some evidence that adaptive density and confidence-based aggregation matter, and that the proposed detection decoder improves perceptual metrics relative to dense pixel-aligned variants.

The paper is mostly clear and includes relevant implementation details in the supplement, including backbone choice, decoder structure, heatmap temperature, input channels, and focal-length/depth analyses.
weaknesses: The central novelty is somewhat incremental. The method combines a very strong pretrained VGGT backbone with known ideas from keypoint heatmap regression, entropy-based adaptive patch allocation, and confidence pruning. The paper does not fully isolate how much of the gain comes from the off-grid primitive formulation versus VGGT fine-tuning, training data, losses, or evaluation protocol.

The evaluation protocol for pose-free novel view synthesis is concerning. Target camera poses are obtained by a second forward pass that includes the target views, which means target images influence the pose used for rendering. This may be common in this subarea, but it weakens the interpretation of the reported NVS numbers and favors methods with strong pose predictors such as VGGT-based systems.

The empirical evidence is narrower and more mixed than the claims suggest. On Charge sparse settings, the proposed method is not consistently best, often trailing VGGT+DepthSplat or FLARE on PSNR/SSIM. The paper explains this partly via cropping/background issues, but the headline claim of state-of-the-art rendering is therefore not uniformly supported.

The geometry-improvement claim is only partially supported. Table 2 shows improved camera pose AUC over VGGT, but depth metrics on Charge are worse than the original VGGT in AbsRel and delta<1.25 for all reported view counts. The supplement’s focal-length results are also mixed on Charge. The paper should temper claims that rendering supervision improves the 3D foundation model broadly.

Efficiency is asserted but not convincingly quantified. The paper reports fewer primitives, but gives little direct evidence on wall-clock inference time, rendering FPS, GPU memory, training cost, or quality-efficiency Pareto curves. Since efficiency is a major claimed advantage, primitive count alone is insufficient.

Baseline fairness is not fully convincing. The closest comparison is AnySplat, but it is unclear whether all baselines are retrained, evaluated with identical preprocessing, alignment, target-pose handling, and data exposure. The paper also lacks stronger oracle or controlled baselines, such as pose-known evaluation, VGGT with alternative lightweight decoders, or the same decoder without VGGT fine-tuning.

The adaptive density mechanism appears heuristic: fixed entropy thresholds and primitive counts are chosen without much justification or sensitivity analysis. This makes it hard to know whether the contribution is robust or tuned for the chosen resolution/datasets.

Reproducibility remains limited. Key training details such as loss weights, optimizer, schedule, number of iterations, dataset sampling proportions, full preprocessing, and rasterizer specifics are either missing or underspecified. The requirement of a 140 GB GPU also raises practical barriers to reproduction.

The paper’s limitations section is too narrow. It mentions missing unseen regions but does not discuss dependence on VGGT failure modes, target-view pose estimation assumptions, robustness to dynamic scenes or specular/transparent content, calibration errors, or the risk that confidence pruning removes valid but hard-to-render structure.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: rigid pixel- or voxel-aligned primitive placement. The proposed continuous, heatmap-based primitive detection is a clean and technically plausible idea, and it is well motivated by the redundancy and artifacts of dense regular grids.

The method is compelling as a system: it combines sub-pixel primitive localization, entropy-based adaptive density, confidence-weighted multi-view fusion, and self-supervised fine-tuning of a VGGT backbone. These components fit together coherently rather than feeling like unrelated additions.

The empirical results are generally strong. On DL3DV the method improves over AnySplat, FLARE, and VGGT+DepthSplat on most reported novel-view metrics while using substantially fewer Gaussians. The efficiency gain is especially convincing: e.g., far fewer primitives than voxel/pixel-aligned alternatives at comparable or better quality.

The paper includes useful ablations showing that adaptive density and learned confidence improve performance, and that detected primitives outperform pixel-aligned variants especially in SSIM/LPIPS and visual artifacts.

The geometry evaluation is a valuable addition. Showing that rendering-based self-supervised fine-tuning improves camera pose estimation over VGGT while avoiding the geometry degradation observed for AnySplat strengthens the contribution beyond image synthesis quality alone.
The manuscript is clear overall, with helpful diagrams and qualitative comparisons that make the primitive allocation behavior and artifact reduction easy to understand.
weaknesses: The strongest claims should be slightly tempered. On Charge, VGGT+DepthSplat is better for several sparse-view PSNR/SSIM settings, and AnySplat has better LPIPS in the 25-view Charge setup. The method is clearly competitive and often better, but not uniformly state of the art across all reported metrics and datasets.

The evaluation breadth is moderate. Results are mainly on DL3DV and Charge; both are relevant, but the paper would be stronger with more diverse real-world out-of-distribution scenes, object-centric settings, and stress cases involving thin structures, reflective surfaces, sky/backgrounds, and wide-baseline extrapolation.

The test-time alignment protocol is somewhat delicate: target images are used in a second forward pass to obtain target camera poses. This may be standard for pose-free evaluation, but it complicates interpretation of novel-view synthesis performance and should be discussed more explicitly as an evaluation assumption.

The ablation evidence supports the components, but some conclusions are not fully clean. The pixel-aligned baseline has similar PSNR to the full method in Table 3, and the largest gains appear in SSIM/LPIPS; this is still meaningful, but the paper should avoid implying large gains on all metrics.

Reproducibility is only partial from the manuscript. Important implementation details such as loss weights, optimizer settings, training schedule, dataset sampling proportions, exact preprocessing, and custom rasterizer details are not sufficiently specified in the main paper, and training requires a very large 140GB GPU.

The method depends heavily on VGGT-1B and datasets overlapping with those used by VGGT/AnySplat training. This is reasonable for the problem setting, but it makes it harder to isolate how much improvement comes from the proposed decoder versus backbone/data advantages.

Limitations are somewhat underdeveloped. The paper mentions holes in unobserved regions, but other likely failure modes such as inaccurate depth in far backgrounds, crop-induced context loss, dynamic objects, calibration errors, and memory/scaling behavior with many views deserve more direct analysis.

strengths: The paper addresses an important bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: rigid pixel/voxel-aligned primitive placement. The proposed off-grid heatmap/DSNT-style primitive detection is technically plausible, differentiable, and well matched to the stated goal of decoupling primitive count from image resolution.

The empirical results are strong for the claimed setting. Across six evaluation datasets, the method substantially improves over the closest VGGT-based baseline AnySplat and DA3-Giant in average PSNR/SSIM/LPIPS while using far fewer primitives per input pixel.

The ablations support the main design choices: off-grid placement improves over pixel-aligned and pixel+offset variants, self-rendering improves perceptual quality, and adaptive density plus confidence pruning improves DL3DV metrics.

The method is clearly motivated and the paper gives useful qualitative evidence, including extrapolated views, confidence maps, learned heatmap behavior, and depth comparisons, which help explain why the representation is cleaner than voxel- or pixel-aligned alternatives.

The contribution is practically useful: compact feed-forward 3DGS reconstruction from unposed images is a relevant direction, and a 7x reduction in primitives with improved rendering quality is meaningful even if not every efficiency aspect is fully measured.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol uses target images in a second forward pass to obtain target camera poses for novel-view evaluation. Even if the Gaussian model itself is built from context views, this target-dependent pose estimation is a nonstandard form of test-time access and could make the NVS evaluation less comparable to settings where target poses are given or estimated only from context. The paper should more carefully justify this and quantify sensitivity to pose-estimation errors or alternative alignment protocols.

Reproducibility is incomplete. The paper omits key training details such as exact dataset subsets and held-out splits, optimizer, learning rate schedule, training duration, batch construction specifics, full loss formula and weights, rasterizer details, and hardware/runtime measurements beyond mentioning a 140GB GPU. These omissions matter because the method depends on large-scale fine-tuning and several interacting losses.

The efficiency claims are only partially supported. The primitive count reduction is reported, but there is no systematic table for inference time, rendering FPS, memory, training cost, or scaling with number of views/resolution. Since efficiency is a central motivation, fewer Gaussians alone does not fully establish practical speed or memory advantages.

The comparison set is somewhat narrow. AnySplat and DA3-Giant are relevant, but the paper does not include several other pose-free/feed-forward or pose-known upper-bound baselines in the main quantitative table, nor does it show how much of the gain comes from VGGT fine-tuning versus the decoder under identical compute and training data.

The adaptive-density mechanism is hand-designed using grayscale entropy thresholds and fixed primitive counts. It works empirically, but the paper gives limited analysis of threshold sensitivity, learned alternatives, behavior on texture-rich but geometrically simple regions, or failure cases where entropy may allocate primitives poorly.

The ablations are useful but not comprehensive. Primitive-placement ablations are reported only on two datasets, while adaptive density/confidence is reported only on DL3DV; per-view-count breakdowns are absent despite averaging over 3/6/9/12 views. This makes it harder to assess robustness across sparse versus denser input regimes.

The method remains strongly dependent on VGGT geometry and teacher regularization. The paper acknowledges depth failures and shows fine-tuning helps, but does not fully characterize when inherited geometry errors dominate, how robust the system is out of distribution, or whether the decoder works similarly with other reconstruction backbones.

Presentation is generally clear, but there are several polish issues and ambiguities: missing project-page link, a broken SCRREAM citation marker, typos, undefined or lightly specified loss weights, and some claims such as state-of-the-art and seconds-level generation are stronger than the reported evidence directly supports.

strengths: The paper targets an important bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: rigid pixel- or voxel-aligned primitive placement. The proposed off-grid DSNT-style primitive detection is a plausible and technically coherent way to decouple primitive locations from the image grid.

The reported quantitative gains are substantial: Table 1 shows consistent improvements over AnySplat and DA3-Giant across six datasets, while using far fewer Gaussians per input pixel. The ablations in Tables 3 and 4 support that off-grid placement, adaptive density, confidence pruning, and self-rendering each contribute to the final result.

The method is conceptually simple and potentially useful: using entropy-based adaptive density and confidence-weighted multi-view aggregation is easy to understand and could be relevant beyond this exact VGGT-based system.

The paper includes helpful qualitative comparisons and acknowledges several limitations, including incomplete unseen geometry, view-dependent appearance, lighting variation, and poor handling of humans.
weaknesses: The central contribution is not fully disentangled from the very strong VGGT backbone and large-scale fine-tuning. The paper claims state-of-the-art feed-forward 3DGS, but much of the performance may come from VGGT geometry, photometric fine-tuning, and training data scale rather than the off-grid primitive detector itself. The ablations help, but they are limited and do not fully isolate backbone, training data, and decoder effects.

The evaluation protocol is concerning: target camera poses are obtained by a second forward pass that includes the target images. Even if the target images are not used to build the Gaussian model, using them to estimate target poses introduces transductive information into novel-view evaluation and makes the reported rendering metrics harder to interpret as true feed-forward NVS from context views alone.

Reproducibility is weak. Many essential details are missing or deferred: loss weights, optimizer, schedule, number of iterations, dataset sizes/subsets, data sampling proportions, exact pruning behavior, runtime, memory, and details of the custom rasterizer. Training requires a 140GB GPU, which also limits independent verification.

The efficiency claim is mostly supported by number of primitives, not by measured wall-clock rendering speed, memory footprint, training cost, or latency. Fewer Gaussians per pixel is promising, but the paper does not sufficiently demonstrate practical system-level efficiency.

The novelty is moderate. The paper combines known ingredients: DSNT/soft-argmax keypoint localization, entropy-based adaptive allocation, confidence pruning, U-Net decoding, VGGT fine-tuning, and standard 3DGS rendering losses. The resulting system may work well, but the paper overstates the originality of the individual technical components.

The comparison set is narrow for some claims. The main table compares only two pose-free feed-forward baselines, and the ablations are reported only on Tanks and Temples/MipNeRF360 or DL3DV. There is no comparison to stronger posed or optimization-based 3DGS where appropriate, nor enough analysis of failure modes across scene types.

Some claims are not adequately evidenced. For example, the paper states that the method produces cleaner geometry and improves VGGT, but the geometry metrics in Table 2 are mixed: DA3-Giant has better depth and pose on average, and the improvements over VGGT are not uniformly large.

Presentation issues reduce confidence: there are grammar errors, malformed/missing citations such as SCRREAM in the dataset paragraph, an empty project-page placeholder, and dense tables with poor readability. These are not the main reason for rejection, but they reinforce the impression that the submission is not yet mature.

strengths: The paper tackles an important bottleneck in feed-forward 3D Gaussian Splatting: rigid pixel- or voxel-aligned primitive placement. The proposed off-grid DSNT-style primitive detection is a clear, technically plausible way to decouple Gaussian count and location from the input pixel grid.

The method is well motivated and integrates several complementary mechanisms: sub-pixel primitive detection, entropy-based adaptive patch density, confidence-based multi-view pruning, self-rendering, and geometry/teacher regularization for stable pose-free training.

The empirical results are strong for the paper's stated setting. Table 1 reports consistent gains over AnySplat and DepthAnything3 across six datasets, with a large average PSNR/SSIM improvement over AnySplat while using far fewer primitives (#G/pix 0.143 versus 0.814/1.0).

Ablations support the main design choices. The off-grid decoder improves over pixel-aligned and pixel-plus-offset variants, while adaptive density and confidence pruning each materially affect quality, especially LPIPS.

The work is potentially useful: compact feed-forward Gaussian prediction from unposed images is practically attractive, and the visual comparisons suggest cleaner extrapolated geometry than voxel-aligned baselines.
weaknesses: The evaluation protocol for pose-free novel view synthesis is somewhat delicate: target camera poses are estimated using a second forward pass that includes target views. Although the authors state this follows AnySplat and does not optimize through rendering, it makes the benchmark partly transductive and complicates comparison to settings where target images are unavailable except for evaluation.

Efficiency claims are not fully quantified. The paper reports primitive count reduction, but does not give enough runtime, memory, rendering speed, or training/inference cost analysis to establish the practical gains implied by the compact representation, especially with a VGGT-1B backbone and 140GB-GPU training.

The main comparison set is narrow. The strongest table compares primarily to AnySplat and DepthAnything3; broader comparisons to relevant feed-forward 3DGS/generalizable NVS systems, or more careful discussion of why they are excluded, would make the state-of-the-art claim more convincing.

Reproducibility is incomplete from the manuscript. Important details such as exact training dataset subsets, sampling counts, optimizer, schedule, loss weights, batch composition, and code availability are insufficiently specified; the project page placeholder is blank in the manuscript.

Some design choices are heuristic and only partially analyzed, including fixed entropy thresholds for adaptive density, fixed primitive counts per patch, the alpha-confidence pruning threshold, and the entropy measure itself. A compression-quality curve or learned/allocation baseline would strengthen the case.

The method inherits limitations from the reconstruction backbone and visible-surface assumption. The paper acknowledges holes in unseen regions, reduced handling of view-dependent appearance, and poor human-subject performance, which may limit deployment in common dynamic or reflective scenes.
